target: AG1’s claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, accessibility, workplace safety, and productivity
objection: The benefits of AI come with serious social costs that often fall on ordinary people, so AI is not broadly good for society in a reliable sense.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps the economy by automating routine tasks and increasing productivity
objection: Automation is not neutral: it can reduce workers’ income and bargaining power, while gains concentrate in large firms that own the data and infrastructure.

target: AG1’s implication that AI improves health outcomes
objection: AI-driven medical decisions are often opaque and trained on biased or incomplete data, which can produce unequal health outcomes rather than better care for everyone.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves accessibility for marginalized people through assistive tools
objection: Accessibility tools can depend on intrusive collection of sensitive personal data such as voice, images, and location, so the accessibility benefit can come at the cost of privacy and surveillance.

target: AG1’s claim that AI improves workplace safety
objection: AI safety systems can fail silently, misclassify situations, or be used to shift responsibility away from companies, creating new risks instead of simply reducing accidents.

target: AG1’s claim that AI helps students and professionals without major downsides
objection: AI use can weaken critical thinking because people may outsource drafting, problem-solving, and fact-checking to the system, eroding their independent reasoning skills.

target: AG1’s overall positive view of AI’s social impact
objection: AI systems can repeat and amplify societal racism because they learn from biased historical data, worsening outcomes for racial minorities in areas like hiring, lending, policing-adjacent tools, education, and recommendations.

target: AG1’s claim that the harms of AI can be managed through guardrails and policy
objection: The safeguards AG1 relies on are hard to enforce and unlikely to scale, because companies are incentivized to collect data, deploy quickly, and cut labor costs rather than adopt costly protections.

target: AG1’s suggestion that human oversight can reliably prevent AI harm in healthcare and other high-stakes settings
objection: Human oversight is not a dependable fix because it requires time, staffing, and training that many deployments lack, so it often becomes a rubber stamp that shifts blame after failures.

target: AG1’s claim that AI literacy and better assignment design can preserve critical thinking in education and work
objection: Even with improved pedagogy, people still have incentives to use AI to generate answers quickly, so outsourcing and critical-thinking erosion will persist unless the system is policed in intrusive ways.

target: AG1’s claim that bias can be adequately reduced through auditing, better datasets, fairness constraints, and documentation
objection: Bias mitigation has limits because it cannot eliminate bias rooted in unequal social systems, and affected groups often lack meaningful recourse when AI causes harm.

target: AG1’s assumption that privacy concerns can be solved through privacy-by-design and consent controls
objection: In practice, privacy tradeoffs are often unavoidable because assistive, healthcare, and enterprise tools usually require sensitive data pipelines, and consent can be nominal when users have few alternatives.

target: AG1’s claim that governance and accountability can realign AI incentives enough to make it broadly beneficial
objection: Incentives, weak enforceability, and profit motives make responsible use unreliable at scale, so the harms are structural rather than mere technical bugs.

target: AG1’s claim that audit, liability, and regulatory requirements can keep AI deployment safe
objection: Governance cannot realistically keep up with fast-changing, opaque AI systems, and liability often fails to clearly assign responsibility when harms emerge from complex pipelines.

target: AG1’s confidence that stronger institutions can prevent AI harm despite market pressures
objection: Regulatory capture and global competition push oversight toward weak, box-ticking compliance rather than strong protections, so enforceable rules are not as reliable as AG1 suggests.

target: AG1’s suggestion that AI can also fight misinformation and fraud with detection and security tools
objection: AI creates scalable new harms such as automated misinformation, deepfakes, fraud, and identity risk, and these problems persist even when individual systems are made safer.

target: AG1’s claim that continuous monitoring, provenance tools, and detection can control AI’s new harms
objection: Continuous monitoring increases surveillance pressure and privacy harms, provenance and detection face a cat-and-mouse problem, and fraud mitigation often requires more centralized data sharing, so the fixes can reproduce the same harms they are meant to solve.

target: AG1’s claim that privacy-preserving analytics and risk-tiered oversight can avoid surveillance harms
objection: Privacy-preserving monitoring still requires enough data to detect misuse, which pushes toward surveillance-by-architecture and concentrates power in large platforms and vendors.

target: AG1’s claim that cryptographic provenance and signing can solve misinformation problems
objection: Provenance only works if major platforms and distribution channels adopt and honor verification, and it can become a gatekeeping system that risks biased enforcement against marginalized groups.

target: AG1’s claim that layered technical defenses can keep pace with malicious AI use
objection: Even with stronger detectors, attackers can generate new persuasive variants cheaply, so defense cannot close the gap between scalable abuse and scalable protection.

target: AG1’s overall net-benefit framing of AI as a broadly positive technology
objection: If making AI beneficial requires constant, sophisticated governance, centralized monitoring, and ecosystem-wide compliance, then AI’s default societal impact is not reliably positive.

target: AG2’s claim that AI’s harms make it broadly bad for society because automation, bias, privacy risks, safety failures, and reduced critical thinking outweigh benefits
objection: The harms are real, but they are not inevitable and can be managed so that AI remains broadly beneficial.

target: AG2’s claim that automation necessarily harms workers and small businesses
objection: AI can also create new kinds of work and raise productivity, and with retraining, wage supports, and job-creation incentives, economic disruption need not be net harm.

target: AG2’s claim that AI worsens health outcomes because models are opaque and biased
objection: Health harms can be reduced through evaluation on diverse populations, ongoing monitoring, explainability where appropriate, and human clinician oversight, allowing AI to support earlier detection and more consistent care.

target: AG2’s claim that accessibility tools are undermined by privacy and surveillance
objection: Accessibility and privacy are not mutually exclusive: assistive tools can be built with privacy-by-design features such as on-device processing, minimal data retention, encryption, and user consent controls.

target: AG2’s claim that AI safety tools are unreliable because systems can fail or shift responsibility to users
objection: Safety can be improved through redundancy, testing, audits, incident reporting, and clear accountability, so AI can reduce hazards when integrated into robust procedures.

target: AG2’s claim that AI necessarily weakens critical thinking by helping with school and work tasks
objection: AI can support critical thinking if it is used as a tutor that asks students to explain steps, verify sources, and work through reasoning rather than simply producing answers.

target: AG2’s claim that AI inevitably amplifies racial bias
objection: Bias can be reduced through bias auditing, better datasets, fairness constraints, transparent documentation, and recourse for affected users.

target: AG2’s claim that safeguards cannot scale because incentives favor misuse
objection: Incentives can be realigned through enforceable requirements, liability, procurement rules, and penalties, so responsible behavior does not have to depend only on voluntary goodwill.

target: AG2’s claim that risk management proves AI is not good for society
objection: Many beneficial technologies, such as healthcare, aviation, and workplace safety systems, also require governance, so the need for oversight does not imply the technology is harmful overall.

target: AG2’s claim that human oversight is too weak to matter
objection: Oversight can be layered with technical safeguards such as monitoring for error patterns, escalation triggers, constrained outputs in high-stakes contexts, and continuous evaluation rather than relying on busy humans alone.

target: AG2’s claim that AI use in education inevitably erodes critical thinking
objection: Schools and workplaces can design assignments and evaluations around reasoning, checkpoints, oral defense, and verification tasks so AI becomes a learning aid instead of a shortcut.

target: AG2’s claim that governance cannot keep up with AI’s rapid changes and opaque deployment
objection: Oversight can be continuous rather than one-time, using monitoring, update notifications, red-teaming, and incident reporting to track a moving target.

target: AG2’s claim that AI mainly worsens misinformation and manipulation
objection: The same AI that generates synthetic content can also detect it, add provenance, and support rapid verification workflows, so new risks do not automatically mean net harm.

target: AG2’s claim that AI mainly increases fraud and identity risk
objection: AI can also improve authentication, anomaly detection, account-takeover detection, and real-time security monitoring, which can reduce fraud-related harm.

target: AG2’s claim that regulatory capture makes stronger AI governance unrealistic
objection: Regulatory capture is a reason to build better institutions, such as independent auditing bodies, transparency requirements, and liability mechanisms, not a reason to conclude AI is inherently socially harmful.

target: AG2’s claim that continuous monitoring necessarily means mass surveillance
objection: Monitoring can be targeted and privacy-preserving through risk-tiered oversight, data minimization, encryption, short retention, and techniques like differential privacy or federated approaches.

target: AG2’s claim that provenance and watermarking cannot work in practice
objection: Provenance can be layered with cryptographic signing, pipeline auditing, and workflow-based verification, so it is not limited to a single fragile detector.

target: AG2’s claim that attackers will always outpace AI defenses
objection: The cat-and-mouse dynamic cuts both ways because defenders can also use AI to scale detection, moderation, and response, especially with mandatory evaluation and robust systems.

target: AG2’s claim that only large institutions can afford effective safeguards
objection: Unequal capacity is a policy design problem that can be addressed with shared standards, independent compliance tools, and procurement requirements, allowing smaller providers to meet baseline protections.
